# TITAN, from Fortran to Julia {#sec-titan-port}

## Why TITAN {#sec-why-titan}

The steady model of the previous chapters leaves three questions to dynamics: which branch nature selects, whether
either is stable, and what happens past the fold. These need implicit radiation hydrodynamics that can resolve a
radiating accretion shock on top of a hydrostatic, radiation-dominated envelope. TITAN [@gehmeyr1994] was built for
this kind of problem. It is one-dimensional, fully implicit, and solves the comoving-frame grey radiation
hydrodynamics of @mihalas1984 on an adaptive Dorfi–Drury grid [@dorfi1987]. Its radiating-shock benchmarks are the
standard ones [@sincell1999a; @sincell1999b]. The 1995 release (version 1.2) is Fortran 77 written for Crays and SGI
workstations.

## The equations TITAN solves {#sec-titan-eqs}

Each zone carries seven unknowns: the radius $r$ and exterior mass $m_e$ at interfaces, the density $\rho$ and gas
temperature $T$ at zone centres, the velocity $u$ at interfaces, the radiation energy density $E$ at centres, and the
comoving radiative flux $F$ at interfaces. Schematically (spherical-geometry terms abbreviated, $O(v/c)$, grey), in
conservative form on a moving mesh with $u_{\rm rel} = u - \dot r$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{d}{dt}\int\rho\,dV + \oint\rho\,u_{\rm rel}\,dA = 0, \\
&\frac{d}{dt}\int\rho u\,dV + \oint\rho u\,u_{\rm rel}\,dA + \int\Big(\nabla p + \rho\frac{Gm}{r^2} - \frac{\rho\chi_F}{c}F + \nabla\!\cdot Q\Big)dV = 0,\\
&\frac{d}{dt}\int\rho\Big(e + \frac{E}{\rho}\Big)dV + \oint\big(\rho e + E\big)u_{\rm rel}\,dA
 + \int\Big[(p + fE)\,\nabla\!\cdot u + \nabla\!\cdot F + Q\!:\!\nabla u\Big]dV = 0,\\
&\frac{d}{dt}\int E\,dV + \oint E\,u_{\rm rel}\,dA + \int\Big[\nabla\!\cdot F + fE\,\nabla\!\cdot u
 + c\,\rho\big(\kappa_E E - 4\pi\kappa_P B/c\big)\Big]dV = 0,\\
&\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{D F}{Dt} + \nabla(fE) + \frac{3f - 1}{r}E + \frac{\rho\chi_F}{c}F = 0 ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-titan}

plus the grid equation that places the interfaces. The second energy equation is the gas plus radiation energy.
TITAN discretises each term in its own way; the Julia residuals reproduce those discretisations term by term. The Eddington factor $f = K/J$ comes from a static formal
solution of the transfer equation along tangent rays. $Q$ is a tensor artificial viscosity, and $\theta$-centring in
time makes the scheme implicit. Every equation is a residual; Newton–Raphson on all unknowns at once, with a
block-pentadiagonal Jacobian, advances one step.

## How the port was done {#sec-port-method}

The port went in phases, each verified before the next began. Bitwise identity was used only as a debugging aid:
the Julia code may use its own mathematics library, automatic differentiation and better linear algebra, so
acceptance is judged on physics.

1. **Fortran as a library.** The original builds with gfortran after one fix. It reproduces the 1995 step counts of
   every benchmark that ends at a fixed time, exactly, about 60–150 times faster than the SGI Indigo2 of 1995
   **[computed]**. Built as a shared library driven from Julia, it is bitwise identical to the standalone code.
2. **Julia residuals with an automatic-differentiation Jacobian.** All seven equations are written once, as
   residuals. One stencil-coloured ForwardDiff sweep produces the Jacobian, which agrees with TITAN's hand-coded one to
   $2\times10^{-11}$ of the row maximum. TITAN drops a few derivatives by design; the AD Jacobian is exact.
3. **Every routine of the time step.** The predictor, the Newton update, the time-step control, the energy
   diagnostic, the formal solution for the Eddington factors and the block solver were each translated. Each was then
   checked *in flight*: on every call during a full run, the Fortran and Julia versions start from the same snapshot
   of every COMMON variable, and every output variable is compared. All agree to $\le 2\times10^{-11}$; the one
   outlier traces to a single last-bit difference of `pow` between Julia and glibc.
4. **No Fortran at run time.** The model state lives in Julia arrays. A benchmark's initial state is captured once
   from the Fortran set-up and stored in a 35–63 kB file, and the run needs no Fortran library at all.

Acceptance has three tiers:

- **(a)** per routine, $10^{-12}$;
- **(b)** per step, the Newton tolerance $10^{-5}$;
- **(c)** physical observables, interpolated to fixed times: positions within 0.5 % of a length scale,
  temperatures within 1 %, step counts within 3 %.

Tier (c) exists because the time-step history of an implicit code is chaotic at the level of round-off. The 1995
README already reports different results on different machines.

| problem | pure Julia steps | Fortran (bookkeeping fixed) | tier (c) | ms/step, Julia | ms/step, Fortran |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SOD shock tube | 455 | 452 | accept | 2.4 | 6.4 |
| SUBC subcritical radiating shock | 587 | 587 | accept | 4.7 | 6.7 |
| SUPC supercritical radiating shock | 713 | 713 | accept | 4.3–5.0 | 6.4 |

: The benchmarks run entirely in Julia **[computed]**. Two bookkeeping fixes (the clock after a rejected step,
and when the energy diagnostic is booked) change the step at which $t_{\max}$ is reached, not the solution. {#tbl-bench}

## What was added for quasi-stars {#sec-titan-additions}

TITAN 1.2 has no convection, no realistic equation of state and no tabulated opacities. No benchmark uses gravity,
a central mass or an inflow boundary, so those paths had never been exercised.

- **Pluggable materials.** The zero-metallicity Saha gas of @sec-saha and the tabulated means of @sec-opacity enter
  through one interface, used both inside the AD residual and in the state updates. ForwardDiff differentiates
  through the Saha solve. A Newton polish of the charge balance keeps the derivatives exact, and the nested AD tags
  are ordered explicitly. The coloured Jacobian equals the dense AD Jacobian exactly, and finite differences to
  $1.5\times10^{-6}$ **[computed]**.
- **A local mixing-length convective flux** in the energy equation, with $\alpha = 0.8$ as in MESA-QUEST. For a time-dependent code the
  natural form is the flux at a given actual gradient $\nabla$, from the same theory as @eq-mlt-cubic:

  $$
  F_{\rm conv} = \rho\,c_P T\sqrt{g\delta}\,\frac{\ell^2\zeta^3}{4\sqrt2\,H_P^{3/2}},\qquad \zeta = \sqrt{U^2 + \nabla - \nabla_{\rm ad}} - U .
  $$ {#eq-fconv}

  It is smooth at onset ($\propto\zeta^3$). It is switched off above Rosseland optical depth 1, because mixing-length
  theory is a diffusion-limit theory: without the cut, the optically thin atmosphere convects spuriously, since there
  $P \approx fE$ is nearly constant and $\nabla$ is ill-defined.
- **Gravity of a central mass**, an imposed luminosity at the inner boundary, a prescribed inflow state at the outer
  boundary, and the physical constants of the steady model. TITAN's own constants differ by up to $2\times10^{-4}$,
  which matters when the net force is 1 % of gravity.
